content: Chemical pneumonitis refers to inflammation of the lung tissue caused by exposure to various irritants. These irritants may include aspirated vomitus, barium used in gastrointestinal imaging, ingested gasoline or other petroleum distillates, pesticides absorbed through ingestion or skin contact, gases released during electroplating, or other chemical irritants. It is important to note that chemical pneumonitis is not an infectious condition. When the causative agent is an oil-based substance, the condition is specifically referred to as lipoid pneumonitis. Mendelson's syndrome is a specific type of chemical pneumonitis that occurs due to the aspiration of gastric acid. This syndrome was first identified in pregnant women who aspirated gastric contents during anesthesia, leading to respiratory distress, cyanosis, and the appearance of lung infiltrates on chest X-rays. The causes of chemical pneumonitis are diverse and include exposure to aspirated vomitus, barium used in imaging studies, ingested petroleum products such as gasoline, pesticides absorbed through ingestion or skin contact, inhalation of gases from electroplating processes, and other chemical irritants. Inhalant use can also be a contributing factor. When the irritant is oil-based, the condition is termed lipoid pneumonitis. The natural history and prognosis of chemical pneumonitis vary. Approximately 60% of patients experience clinical improvement, with resolution of abnormalities on chest X-rays. However, about one-third of patients initially show rapid improvement, only to develop new progressive lung infiltrates later. This suggests the possibility of a secondary bacterial infection or the onset of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). The least common but most severe outcome is the development of fulminant disease, which can result in acute death.
